name: Malaria

likely: Plasmodium ovale (less common in South Asia)
pathogens.why: P. falciparum and P. vivax account for the large majority of malaria in India; species identification on smear/RDT is essential since management, monitoring for severity, and radical cure (primaquine for P. vivax) differ significantly by species.

investigations.test: Peripheral blood smear (thick and thin film)
investigations.why: Gold standard for diagnosis, species identification, and parasitemia quantification — directly determines treatment choice and monitoring.
Fast bedside screening tool, useful when smear is not immediately available, though species specificity is more limited than smear.
Thrombocytopenia is a common supportive finding; hemoglobin helps assess severity (severe anemia is a marker of complicated malaria).

investigations.test: Renal function tests, blood glucose, LFTs
investigations.why: Screens for organ dysfunction that would classify this as severe/complicated malaria requiring IV therapy and higher level of care.
Acidosis is a severity marker in falciparum malaria with prognostic significance.

references: National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP) India Guidelines
reasonSource: ()=>"Fever with chills/rigors, thrombocytopenia and/or splenomegaly in a patient from or travelling through an endemic area is most consistent with malaria — a protozoal infection. Antibiotics have no role here; the priority is urgent peripheral smear/rapid diagnostic testing and prompt antimalarial therapy specific to the Plasmodium species identified, since delay (especially in P. falciparum) can progress rapidly to severe/complicated malaria."
